item.title: Cawaci draws rugby strength into hockey challenge
item.description: SAINT John’s College Cawaci is confident of making a strong challenge for the hockey title, with the school’s boys’ team drawing on the fitness and experience of players who have recently completed the rugby season. Cawaci competes in the Fiji Secondary Schools Hockey Championships with four teams, featuring the Under-16 girls and boys and Under-19 girls and boys’ categories.
item.content:encoded:
SAINT John’s College Cawaci is confident of making a strong challenge for the hockey title, with the school’s boys’ team drawing on the fitness and experience of players who have recently completed the rugby season.

Cawaci competes in the Fiji Secondary Schools Hockey Championships with four teams, featuring the Under-16 girls and boys and Under-19 girls and boys’ categories.

School teacher Lusiana Hawili said the transition from rugby to hockey had been relatively smooth for the boys, with most of the players already fit and accustomed to playing hockey.

“Most of our boys, since there are fewer numbers in our team, are from the Under-18s. Our preparation was good because since they transitioned from rugby to hockey, they were already fit,” Hawili said.

She said the main areas of focus for the team would be its defence and execution of short corners.

“We need to focus on our defence. We must be careful with our defence and our short corners. Other than that, I have a good feeling we’ll take back something to Cawaci”

Cawaci’s Under-19 boys reached the final last year but went down to Levuka Public School.

Hawili said that defeat had motivated the players to go one step further this year.

“We reached the finals and we lost to LPS. We are just encouraging the boys that we can win this year,” she said.

She added that many of the players had been involved in hockey since Under-16 level while also playing rugby, making the transition between the two sports easier.

“Most of them have been playing hockey from Under-16 and they are also joining the rugby team. After the rugby season, they always come and join.”

Hawili also believes hockey continues to develop strongly in Ovalau, despite being regarded as a minor sport in Fiji.

She said all three schools on the island are involved in hockey, with the sport also being passed down through families.

“It has been developing very well because in Ovalau, most of all the three schools, St John’s College, Levuka Public School and Delana Methodist High School Levuka, they all play hockey,” she said.

“Most of the students that are playing hockey right now, their parents used to be hockey reps, and they have that urge in them to also play hockey.”

However, Hawili said Cawaci still needed to work on its weaknesses, particularly in defence, to continue improving.

For the girls, her main hope is for the players to enjoy the sport while also challenging for silverware.

“I would just love for them to enjoy the sport and also love for us to take back the trophy since it has been so long,” she said.

Cawaci last lifted the trophy in 2024 after beating Saint Thomas High School 1-nil in the final but fell short in the final last year against Levuka Public School, making this year’s campaign an opportunity to end a wait for success.

item.title: LPS aims to take home silverware
item.description: LEVUKA Public School’s Under-19 girls’ hockey team is determined to make its mark at this year’s Fiji Secondary Schools Hockey Championship. Head coach Simon Vidi saying the side’s main goal is to return to Levuka with something for the school.
item.content:encoded:
LEVUKA Public School’s Under-19 girls’ hockey team is determined to make its mark at this year’s Fiji Secondary Schools Hockey Championship.

Head coach Simon Vidi saying the side’s main goal is to return to Levuka with something for the school.

Vidi said preparations for the tournament were not ideal, with issues at the school initially putting the team’s participation in doubt. However, an agreement with the school principal cleared the way for the girls to compete.

“We started preparing about a month before the tournament,” Vidi said.

The school has a long association with the national secondary school’s hockey competition, having participated since its early years.

Levuka Public also competed in last year’s Fiji Secondary Schools Hockey Championship, which was hosted in Levuka, although the team did not reach the final.

This year, Vidi said the commitment from the players improved as the tournament approached.

“We started with a small group. Last month, we started getting people coming in, so preparation was good,” he said.

The team suffered a narrow 1-0 defeat to St Joseph’s on the opening day, but Vidi said the girls responded positively after a team discussion at camp.

“There’s a big improvement from Day One until today (Thursday). We will improve on the way before the final stages,” he said.

He urged the team’s supporters, particularly former students and the wider Ovalau community living in Lautoka, to get behind the players at Nadovu Park.

“Do come down to support the team,” Vidi said.

“All the Ovalau people out there, make your way down to Lautoka, Nadovu Park. We’ll be waiting.”

Levuka Public School is represented across the competition, with teams in the Under-16 girls’ side as well as an Under-19 boys and girls categories.

item.title: Grammar, Lelean chase Super Deans title
item.description: The long road of Fiji secondary schools rugby reaches its most emotional destination today when Suva Grammar School and Lelean Memorial School meet in the Vodafone Super Deans under-18 final at 6.10pm at HFC Bank Stadium. For these young players, it is more than another rugby match. It is the reward for months of sacrifice, early-morning preparations, bruising training sessions, school commitments
item.content:encoded:
The long road of Fiji secondary schools rugby reaches its most emotional destination today when Suva Grammar School and Lelean Memorial School meet in the Vodafone Super Deans under-18 final at 6.10pm at HFC Bank Stadium.

For these young players, it is more than another rugby match. It is the reward for months of sacrifice, early-morning preparations, bruising training sessions, school commitments and the unwavering support of parents, teachers, old scholars and communities.

Under the lights in Suva, two proud rugby institutions will fight for one of the most coveted prizes in Fiji schoolboy rugby.

The Deans competition itself carries almost nine decades of history.

Introduced in 1939, it is Fiji’s oldest competitive rugby tournament and has helped shape generations of players.

The original trophy was donated by the Maori All Blacks team that toured Fiji in 1938.

That history makes tonight’s contest even more significant.

Lelean Memorial School enters the final carrying the weight of a proud province.

The Davuilevu school has won the Deans Trophy 12 times and shared the title on five occasions, with its first triumph coming in 1948.

The current side has the opportunity to restore the trophy to Lelean after a lengthy wait.

Their journey this year has been particularly impressive.

Lelean went into the national semi-finals as the only undefeated U18 team.

They defeated Ratu Navula College 26-5 in the quarter-final before facing a determined Nasinu Secondary School in the semi-final.

The match was tight early, with Lelean leading 5-0 at halftime, but they found another gear after the break and scored four more tries to secure their place in the final.

Grammar’s road has been just as demanding.

The Southern Zone champions survived the elimination stages before producing one of the most emphatic performances of the championship in their semi-final against Ra High School.

Grammar dominated from the opening whistle, controlling possession and the momentum before completing a remarkable 51-0 victory.

That result has sent a clear warning to Lelean.

Grammar have also shown the depth of their program this year, reaching three Super Deans finals.

But tonight, none of those achievements will matter.

And the history of the two schools will disappear into the noise of the stadium once the first whistle is blown.

There is something uniquely emotional about a Deans final.

For the players, this is a moment they have imagined since they first picked up a rugby ball.

Many will never experience another match quite like it.

Behind every player will be a story of someone who helped them reach this point, a parent who travelled to watch, a teacher who encouraged them, a coach who demanded more, or a teammate who pushed them through the difficult days.

The HFC Bank Stadium is expected to provide a fitting backdrop, with rain potentially adding another layer to the occasion.

If the conditions turn wet, the contest could become a battle of patience, discipline and courage.

The ball may become harder to control, the ground heavier and every carry, tackle and kick more demanding.

Yet rain has never stopped Fiji’s school rugby supporters from turning up.

The stadium will carry the colours, songs and voices of the participating proud school communities.

item.title: Eighty minutes from Deans immortality
item.description: THE stage is set. The wait is almost over. For Lelean Memorial School and Suva Grammar School, today’s Vodafone Super Deans Championship under-18 final at HFC Bank National Stadium is more than a schoolboy rugby match.
item.content:encoded:
THE stage is set. The wait is almost over.

For Lelean Memorial School and Suva Grammar School, today’s Vodafone Super Deans Championship under-18 final at HFC Bank National Stadium is more than a schoolboy rugby match.

It is a battle for the holy grail of Fiji secondary schools rugby and an opportunity to rewrite history after years of disappointment.

Both sides stormed into the final with convincing semi-final victories, confirming their place as the two best U18 teams in the competition.

Now, after years of coming close and falling short, they are just 80 minutes away from ending long title droughts.

For Lelean , it has been 12 years since the Deans trophy last found its way to Davuilevu.

For Grammar, the wait has stretched even longer — 21 years since the school last celebrated Deans glory.

And fittingly, two schools whose rivalry has been built through battles across the age grades will now settle the biggest contest of all.

Lelean captain Luke Daunirutu knows the task facing his side.

He identified the Grammar forward pack as the opposition’s most potent weapon, particularly after watching the way it operated in the semi-final.

“Grammar’s forwards last week kept changing their formation and that made it hard the opposition to defend and anticipate what they were going to do,” Daunirutu said.

That unpredictability has been a major focus for Lelean as it prepares for today’s showdown.

Daunirutu said his teammates understood the magnitude of the occasion and what it would take to bring the trophy back to the school.

“We have prepared well for this final and we know it is going to be a tough game,” he said.

But for the Lelean captain, the motivation runs deeper than the school crest on the jersey.

“We are not only representing our school. We are representing our families and the Lord Almighty as well,” he said.

item.title: Late uncle’s memory in mind
item.description: FOR Lelean Memorial School captain Luke Daunitutu, today’s Vodafone Super Deans Championship under-18 final is about more than school pride and the chance to end a 12-year wait for glory. It is also about fulfilling a wish left behind by someone who played a special role in his rugby journey.
item.content:encoded:
FOR Lelean Memorial School captain Luke Daunitutu, today’s Vodafone Super Deans Championship under-18 final is about more than school pride and the chance to end a 12-year wait for glory.

It is also about fulfilling a wish left behind by someone who played a special role in his rugby journey.

The Lelean flanker revealed yesterday that he thinks often of his late uncle whenever he steps onto the rugby field, carrying his memory with him every time he pulls on the jersey.

Daunitutu said his uncle was one of his biggest supporters throughout his rugby career and his encouragement remains a source of motivation as he prepares to lead Lelean against Suva Grammar School at HFC Bank National Stadium today.

“He was a great supporter of my rugby career,” Daunitutu said.

“I think of him a lot every time I step onto the rugby field.”

Those memories will carry even greater meaning today as Daunitutu leads Lelean into a final that could end the school’s 12-year wait for the Deans title.

For the young captain, lifting the coveted trophy would be a fitting way to honour the man who believed in his rugby journey.

“I hope I can lift the title in memory of him,” he said.

That personal motivation adds another layer to an already emotional occasion for Daunitutu, who will not only carry the expectations of Lelean’s students, teachers, old boys and supporters but also the memory of a loved one who helped shape his rugby path.

Lelean enters the final after a convincing semi-final victory and faces a Grammar side that has also shown why it belongs on the biggest stage.

Daunitutu knows the challenge ahead, particularly the strength of the Grammar forward pack, which he identified as one of the team’s biggest weapons.

But beyond the tactics and physical battle, today’s final presents Daunitutu with a moment he has dreamed about — leading his school into a Deans final and potentially lifting the trophy in honour of his late uncle.

For 80 minutes, he will carry the hopes of Lelean.

And in his heart, he will carry someone who can no longer be there to watch him play.

item.title: Nadi held, Suva too strong
item.description: THE McDonald’s Nadi Women were forced to settle for a 24-all draw against a determined Fresh Choice Tailevu side in a thrilling Round 4 clash of the Subrails Marama Cup Championship at Churchill Park in Lautoka yesterday. Nadi captain Laisa Seru said her side knew they were in for a tough battle after an impressive victory over Suva Women’s last weekend at HFC Bank Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
THE McDonald’s Nadi Women were forced to settle for a 24-all draw against a determined Fresh Choice Tailevu side in a thrilling Round 4 clash of the Subrails Marama Cup Championship at Churchill Park in Lautoka yesterday.

Nadi captain Laisa Seru said her side knew they were in for a tough battle after an impressive victory over Suva Women’s last weekend at HFC Bank Stadium.

“We knew this game was going to be a hard game for us, considering a win against Suva last week. We knew the target was going to be on our back, and they really gave us a good game,” Seru said.

Seru admitted her team struggled at times to maintain their defensive discipline and became too casual during crucial periods of the match.

“We were a bit too casual out there. It cost us a few defensive weaknesses and allowed the Tailevu side some choices,” she said.

Seru said the team was reminded at halftime of the importance of protecting their home ground and finishing the match strongly.

“When we went into the changing room at half-time, we were told to protect our ground, considering it’s our home game. We wanted to come out here and hold our fort.”

Although Nadi managed to avoid defeat, Seru acknowledged that the performance was not quite at the level the team expected.

“I guess we did that, but it wasn’t good enough. We came away with a tie, but we’re grateful,” she said.

Seru was pleased with the contribution of Nadi’s impact players, who made an impact after coming onto the field in the second half.

“The impact players did very well. Good carries, good support players. We got some choice in the second half and allowed them to play the game,” she said.

Fresh Choice Tailevu team captain Makereta Tunidau acknowledged her girls for giving out their best and showing their talent in the full 80 minutes.

“Though we could not get a win today, but I am so thankful of the girls for holding the fort till the last whistle and showed out well on the field,” Tunidau said.

Tunidau added the team will return on their drawing board, review their game and prepare stronger for their next match.

With the competition intensifying, both the captains said they would use the result as a learning experience, particularly focusing on tightening their defence before their next match.

item.title: Finalists set for another show
item.description: LAST year’s finalists will meet again in the Extra Fiji Secondary Schools Football Championship Under-15 final after AD Patel College edged Labasa College 4-3 on penalties at Subrail Park yesterday. AD Patel held its nerve in the semi-final shootout to earn another chance at the title and a rematch with Lautoka Central College.
item.content:encoded:
LAST year’s finalists will meet again in the Extra Fiji Secondary Schools Football Championship Under-15 final after AD Patel College edged Labasa College 4-3 on penalties at Subrail Park yesterday.

AD Patel held its nerve in the semi-final shootout to earn another chance at the title and a rematch with Lautoka Central College.

The two schools also met in last year’s final, with Lautoka Central College winning 2-0.

AD Patel coach Avinesh Kumar said his players had improved since that defeat and were ready for another challenge against Lautoka Central.

“Central College have won 2-0. So, we are back. We have improved from last year. We are ready now to take on Central College,” he said.

The coach praised his players for their effort against a Labasa side he described as one of the best teams they had faced in the competition.

“Labasa College was a very tough team, but the boys have given their heart. I am very proud of the boys,” he said.

He admitted there were mistakes in the semi-final but said the team would review its performance before the final.

“We will look into it today and we are ready for the finals,” he said.

The coach said he was proud of his players for giving their best.

“They have given their heart out today,” he said.

item.title: NETBALL FIJI REVIVAL I Tokaduadua carries legacy
item.description: From Namuana, Tavuki in Kadavu, to wearing the Crest Fiji Pearls dress, 20-year-old Vuta Tokaduadua is living a dream built on family, sacrifice and determination. Her first appearance for the Crest Fiji Pearls came during the Spirit Series in Sydney in July, marking a proud moment in a journey she never expected to take.
item.content:encoded:
From Namuana, Tavuki in Kadavu, to wearing the Crest Fiji Pearls dress, 20-year-old Vuta Tokaduadua is living a dream built on family, sacrifice and determination.

Her first appearance for the Crest Fiji Pearls came during the Spirit Series in Sydney in July, marking a proud moment in a journey she never expected to take.

Netball was not always part of Vuta’s plans.

“I wasn’t interested in netball at first,” she said. “My mum used to take me to watch my sisters play. It looked confusing, but they taught me the game. Before long, I was playing for Vatuwaqa Primary School.”

From there, her journey grew from Suva Grammar School to Suva age-group teams and eventually national age-group recognition, including a World Youth Cup trialist call-up.

Her biggest inspiration has been her older sister, Lili Tokaduadua, who now plays professional netball in New Zealand with the Stars.

“It has been a real blessing to share this journey with Lili because she is my role model,” Vuta said. “She motivates me to never give up and to keep chasing my dream while making Mum proud.”

Lili left Fiji at just 15 to pursue her own netball dream. For Vuta, watching her sister make that sacrifice showed her what hard work and commitment could achieve.

But behind Vuta’s journey is a mother who sacrificed everything for her and her sibling.

Her father, the late Aisake Nadolo, a former Fiji basketball and rugby representative, passed away when Vuta was just three years old. His time with her was short, but his sporting legacy remains part of the family.

Her mother, Eleni, raised four children on her own in Kinoya, holding the family together through years of sacrifice and perseverance.

“I am incredibly proud of Vuta,” Eleni said. “Representing Fiji has always been her dream. She is continuing our family tradition of serving the country through sport.”

For Vuta, every time she puts on the Crest Fiji Pearls dress, she thinks of her mother.

“Knowing what Mum has done for me is my biggest motivation every time I step onto the court,” she said. “I want to make her proud because she’s given everything to get me here.”

Now studying for a Certificate in Sports Science at Fiji National University, Vuta sees her Crest Pearls debut as more than just an opportunity to play international netball. It is a chance to learn, grow and honour the people who helped her get there.

“My goal is to learn from the experienced players, improve my game, and give everything I have whenever I step on court.”

And to the young girls across Fiji, her message is simple:

“The road will get tough, but never doubt yourself. Don’t compare your journey to anyone else. You are your own competition.”

From a little girl watching her sisters play, to wearing the colours of Fiji, she now carries her family’s story onto the international stage, with her mother’s sacrifices in her heart and a dream of making Fiji proud.

The Crest Fiji Pearls are now preparing for the Netball World Cup Sydney 2027 Qualifier Oceania, where Fiji will battle for a place on the world stage.

Fiji is ready. The journey to Sydney 2027 starts now.

Netball Fiji continues its Road to Netball World Cup 2027 campaign as it builds towards qualification and the global stage.
